explanation: Choose a middle element as root and recursively build the two sorted halves. The subtree sizes differ by at most one, giving minimum height while preserving the sorted inorder sequence.
timeComplexity: O(n). Each input entry creates exactly one node; balanced range splitting gives logarithmic recursive depth.
spaceComplexity: O(log n) auxiliary stack, plus O(n) output nodes. Balanced recursive calls retain logarithmic depth; n new nodes form the returned tree.
attribution: Unmodified EPIJudge reference source: epi_judge_java_solutions/epi/BstFromSortedArray.java. Original contributors; repository LICENSE: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/).
correctness: Every chosen midpoint separates smaller and larger sorted values into the left and right ranges, preserving the BST inorder contents. Splitting each range into near-equal sizes yields the smallest possible height for that number of nodes.
walkthrough: For [2,4,6,8], choose 6 as root, build 4 with left child 2, and place 8 on the right. The inorder values are unchanged and the height is three, which the adapter returns. JSON arguments are [sortedValues]. The wrapper checks inorder equality then observes the returned tree’s node-counting height, not its root value.
edgeCases: An empty array builds an empty tree of height zero.
Even-sized ranges use the upper middle.
The judge accepts the minimum-height structure after checking its contents.
